newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania, Hungary reopen consulate in Transylvania.
newsitem.headline: Romania, Hungary reopen consulate in Transylvania.

text.p: The foreign ministers of Romania and Hungary on Wednesday reopened a Hungarian consulate in Transylvania's main town shut by dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and proclaimed the gesture a final break with communism.

Hundreds of Romanians and ethnic Hungarians cheered Adrian Severin and Laszlo Kovacs and slapped them on the back as they inaugurated the office in an apartment block in Cluj's main square, opposite a Roman Catholic cathedral.
"The reopening of the Hungarian consulate finally closes an era -- the communist era in the history of the two nations," Kovacs told a news conference after the ceremony.

Kovacs praised Romania's centrist government, elected last November, for promoting cultural and linguistic rights for the 1.6 million-strong Hungarian minority. Two ethnic Hungarians are members of the centrist cabinet.
"More has been achieved in the past eight months than in the previous eight decades," he said.

The two countries signed a treaty last year after generations of mistrust rooted in suspicions that Hungary wanted to restore control over Transylvania, which it held under the Austro-Hungarian empire.
Ceausescu ran one of eastern Europe's most autocratic communist regimes for 23 years before his execution in the 1989 revolt that toppled communism.
He closed the consulate in Cluj, 400 km (250 miles) north of Bucharest, in 1988, when East Germans were fleeing to the West en masse, often using Hungarian and Czechoslovak diplomatic missions.

Under Romania's first post-communist president, leftist Ion Iliescu, relations deteriorated between Romanians and ethnic Hungarians. Four people died in rioting in March 1990 in the town of Tirgu Mures.
The consulate is intended to play a symbolic role as Romanian nationals require no visas to visit Hungary. But ethnic Hungarians saw it as a major achievement.
"I'm happy to have lived to see this day," said Attila, a 55-year-old pastor. "Now we feel so much safer as a minority."

Wednesday's ceremony, which took place next to a statue of 15th century Hungarian King Mathias, sought to portray improved ties after Hungary was invited to start talks on entering an expanded NATO together with Poland and the Czech Republic.
Romania, along with Slovenia, was left on the sidelines after NATO's Madrid summit, but told it had a good chance for inclusion in a 1999 review of expansion. Hungary has backed Romanian membership.
In his address, Severin pledged to proceed with the opening of a Hungarian section at Transylvania's main university in Cluj, one of several moves denounced by Romanian nationalists.
Cluj's fiercely nationalist mayor Gheorghe Funar stayed away from the ceremony.
"I would like to declare the consul persona non grata, but unfortunately I don't have such power," he told Reuters.
